title: Localisation Under Pressure
objective: Manage workforce localisation (Saudization) compliance risk during rapid growth.
subject: Our Nitaqat position is slipping
briefing: Our expansion has relied on experienced expatriate hires, and Saudi staff turnover in front-office roles is high. Our localisation ratio is getting close to the band minimum.

documents.title: Context
documents.body: Falling below the band can restrict visa issuance and some services until restored. Two new properties open in four months with 220 hires planned. Exit interviews cite shift patterns and limited career paths.

steps.prompt: At the recent rate (about -0.8 points a month), in how many months will the ratio reach the minimum? ((33.5 - 32) / 0.8)
steps.solution: About 1.9 months: before the new openings.

options.text: Make localisation a KRI with a warning at 1.5 points above the band; prioritise Saudi hiring for the new properties with a graduate programme; fix shift patterns and career paths to cut turnover.
options.feedback: Addresses the trend and its causes.

options.text: Hire Saudi staff into non-operational roles to lift the ratio quickly.
options.feedback: May meet the number without solving turnover; can also raise compliance questions about genuine employment.

options.text: Wait until the new properties open.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Make localisation a KRI with a warning at 1.5 points above the band; prioritise Saudi hiring for the new properties with a graduate programme; fix shift patterns and career paths to cut turnover.”

steps.prompt: Which root causes should you address?

options.text: Shift patterns unattractive to local candidates
Expansion hiring plan ignores the ratio

debrief.summary: You treated localisation as a strategic people risk, not a headcount trick.
key_points: Track regulatory ratios as KRIs with lead time.
debrief.stronger_approach: Model the ratio for the new openings month by month.
debrief.transfer: Workforce compliance obligations exist in many jurisdictions.

endings.title: Strong outcome
endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome
endings.text: Solid work with gaps. Your manager asks you to revisit one or two points.

endings.title: Needs rework
endings.text: The work needs another pass. Use the debrief and try again when ready.

title: Guest Data and the PDPL
objective: Assess personal data protection compliance across booking channels under Saudi data protection law.
subject: Are we compliant with the PDPL?
briefing: Our guest data flows through our website, two booking platforms, a loyalty app and the property management system. I need to know where we are exposed under the PDPL.

documents.title: Data flow review
documents.body:
- Website captures consent; loyalty app does not record purpose.
- Passport scans retained indefinitely at front desks.
- Guest data shared with a marketing agency abroad without a documented transfer assessment.
- No data inventory.

items.text: Set retention limits for ID documents
Fix consent in the loyalty app

steps.why: Address the highest legal exposure first; the inventory supports everything else and can run in parallel.

steps.prompt: Marketing wants to keep sharing data with the agency while you assess.

options.text: Pause new transfers until the assessment is done; offer to fast-track it within two weeks.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Pause new transfers until the assessment is done; offer to fast-track it within two weeks.”

debrief.summary: You mapped data exposure and prioritised the highest legal risks.
key_points: Know your data before you protect it.
debrief.stronger_approach: Appoint data owners for each channel.
debrief.transfer: Data protection principles are similar under many national laws.

title: Season of Events
objective: Plan for a major event season: demand surge, crowd safety, supplier capacity and pricing risk.
subject: Event season demand
briefing: A season of major events will bring a surge of visitors to Riyadh. Occupancy could exceed 98% for six weeks. How do we capture the opportunity without operational failure?

documents.title: Planning data
documents.body:
- Forecast occupancy 98% (six weeks).
- Laundry supplier capacity: 85% of peak need.
- Agency staff availability uncertain; competitors bidding for the same pool.
- Last year: lobby overcrowding during an event night; one guest injury.

options.why: A commercial question, not the main operational risk.

steps.prompt: Laundry capacity covers 85% of peak. Response?

options.text: Contract a second laundry for the peak and pre-stock extra linen.

outcome.bad: The second laundry had delays one weekend; extra stock covered it.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Contract a second laundry for the peak and pre-stock extra linen.”

steps.prompt: How do you handle crowd safety on event nights?

options.text: Crowd plan with timed arrival windows, extra security, clear routes and a trigger to restrict lobby access.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Crowd plan with timed arrival windows, extra security, clear routes and a trigger to restrict lobby access.”

debrief.summary: You balanced opportunity with operational resilience.
key_points: Peak demand stresses suppliers and people.
Crowd safety needs triggers, not hope.
debrief.stronger_approach: Run a scenario where the event schedule changes at short notice.
debrief.transfer: Peak planning applies to retail holidays and healthcare winters.
